DOCKER BASE IMAGE EOL CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your Dockerfile's base image still supported?

A base image reference can be pinned to an exact content digest and still start from a release line — node:18, python:3.9, ubuntu:20.04 — that its own publisher stopped patching months ago. Pinning stops the reference from being silently repointed; it says nothing about whether anyone is still shipping security fixes for what it points to. Paste your Dockerfile below and this page checks every FROM line's release line against a small, dated end-of-life table.

Nothing is uploaded. The Dockerfile you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own — the end-of-life data is a checked-in snapshot, not a live lookup.

1. Paste one or more Dockerfiles

Copy the contents of each Dockerfile (or Dockerfile.* / *.dockerfile) you want checked.

Paste at least one Dockerfile above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineImage : TagStatusEnd-of-lifeSource

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan every Dockerfile under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any base image is eol or deprecated-image
python3 check.py --warn-days 30   # narrow the eol-soon warning window

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a base image whose release line has already gone end-of-life.

Common questions

Isn't a pinned base image already safe?

Pinning (to a tag or a content digest) only stops the reference from being silently repointed to different bytes. It says nothing about whether the release line those bytes belong to is still receiving security patches from its publisher. A FROM line can be pinned to an exact digest and still be building on a Node, Python, or distro release that stopped getting fixes months ago -- pinning and end-of-life are independent questions.

See Docker Base Image Pin Check for the pinning question specifically.

Where does the end-of-life data come from?

A small, curated table checked into this tool, not a live lookup -- the page and the CLI make no network calls of their own. Each entry names the project whose own release schedule or stated support-length policy it was read from, and whether that date is the project's own published end date (confirmed) or inferred from its policy (estimated). Re-verify any finding against the upstream project's own page before relying on it, especially an estimated one, and especially long after the dataset's own snapshot date shown in the results.

Does a clean scan mean my image has no vulnerabilities?

No. This checks one specific thing: whether the base image's release line, as named by its tag, has passed its publisher's own end-of-life date. It is not a vulnerability scan, does not inspect installed packages, and makes no claim about CVEs present in a supported image.

What if my tag is latest, or I use a private registry image?

A tag of latest (or no tag at all, which resolves to latest) names no fixed release line, so it cannot be checked against a dated table -- it is reported as unknown-tag rather than guessed at. The same applies to any image outside this tool's curated table, including private-registry and custom images: reported as unknown-image, which is not evidence of anything either way.

More: how this compares to a vulnerability scanner, how it compares to checking end-of-life dates by hand, or what to do once a finding comes back end-of-life.

Knowing a release line is still supported doesn't tell you it's pinned against being silently repointed: Docker Base Image Pin Check asks that question of the same FROM line. Once the image itself is sound, Docker Cache Order Check asks whether the same Dockerfile's instruction order busts the build cache, and Kubernetes Rollout Safety Check asks whether deploying the built image drops live requests.

vs-a-vulnerability-scanner.html.text:
← Docker Base Image EOL Check

Docker Base Image EOL Check vs. a Vulnerability Scanner

Related tools, different questions. A vulnerability scanner like Trivy, Grype, or Docker Scout tells you which CVEs are already known and present in your image's installed packages -- it needs the image pulled or built. This checker reads only the FROM line's text and answers a narrower, upstream question in your browser: has that release line itself passed its publisher's own end-of-life date, whether or not a CVE has been filed against it yet.

What each tool is for

A vulnerability scanner pulls or builds your image, enumerates the packages actually installed inside it (OS packages, language dependencies, sometimes application libraries), and matches each one against CVE feeds and vendor advisories. It is broad and grounded in what is really in the image -- exactly the right tool for "what known vulnerabilities does this image currently contain." Running one needs the image itself and a maintained vulnerability database.

This checker does one narrower thing, straight from the text of a Dockerfile: it reads each FROM line's image and tag, and checks the release line they name against a small, dated end-of-life table -- no pull, no build, no CVE database. It catches a case a scanner structurally cannot: a base image with zero currently-known CVEs that is still past end-of-life, because a clean scan only means nothing has been matched yet, and nobody is looking for new issues in an unsupported release line the way they are for a supported one.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
What known CVEs are present in the packages actually installed in my built image?A vulnerability scanner -- that is its entire job, and this tool does not attempt any of it.
Has my FROM line's release line itself passed its publisher's end-of-life date?This checker -- straight from the Dockerfile text, no build or pull needed.
My scanner reports zero CVEs for this image -- am I safe?Not necessarily: a clean scan means nothing known has been matched yet, not that the release line is still receiving fixes. Check this tool too.
I want a pre-build check I can run at the same stage as a linter, before CI builds the image.This checker -- it needs only the Dockerfile text, so it runs earlier in the pipeline than any scan of the built image can.

The two are complementary, not competing: a pipeline can run this checker as an early, cheap gate on the Dockerfile itself, then a vulnerability scanner on the built image for the CVE question this tool does not attempt.

Run the free base image EOL check

Common questions

Should I use this checker or a vulnerability scanner like Trivy?

Different shapes of tool for related but different questions. A vulnerability scanner pulls or builds your image, inspects the packages actually installed inside it, and matches each one against CVE databases -- broad, accurate about what is really there, and it needs the image itself. This checker reads only the Dockerfile text and answers one narrower, upstream question: has the release line named by the FROM tag itself passed its publisher's own end-of-life date. It needs no pull, no build, and no CVE database, and it catches the case a scanner cannot: a base image with zero currently-known CVEs that is still unsupported, because nobody is looking for new ones on it anymore.

If Trivy finds no CVEs, does that mean the base image is still supported?

No, and this is the exact gap this tool exists to close. A scanner reports CVEs that are known and matched in its database as of the scan. A base image release line that has passed end-of-life is not necessarily full of already-known CVEs -- it may show a clean scan today and still be a release nobody is patching, so the next vulnerability discovered in it will never be fixed upstream. A clean vulnerability scan answers 'what is already known to be wrong,' not 'is anyone still going to fix what gets found tomorrow.'

Why would I need this if I already run a scanner in CI?

Speed and a different question, not a replacement. A scanner needs the image built or pulled, which in CI means after your build step; this checker reads the Dockerfile text alone and can run before you even build, catching an end-of-life base image at the same review stage as a linter. It is also the more direct answer to a specific worry -- 'is this release line still supported at all' -- when the scanner's dozens of CVE rows do not directly say so.

Is this page affiliated with Trivy, Grype, or Docker Scout?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Aqua Security (Trivy), Anchore (Grype), or Docker, Inc. (Docker Scout). They are named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using publicly documented facts about how each tool works.

vs-checking-eol-dates-by-hand.html.text:
← Docker Base Image EOL Check

Docker Base Image EOL Check vs. Checking End-of-Life Dates by Hand

A manual check works: open each FROM line's project page and read its support policy. It gets slow the moment there is more than one line to check -- a multi-stage build, a handful of services, or a monorepo full of Dockerfiles. This free tool reads every FROM line you paste at once, in your browser, against a small dated table that names its own source for each entry.

What each approach is for

Checking by hand means finding, for each base image tag, the right page to read -- the project's own release notes or end-of-life policy -- and working out whether today's date is past the line it names. For one Dockerfile with one FROM line this can be the fastest route, and it is the only way to reason about an image outside any curated table.

This checker reads the text of every Dockerfile you paste, pulls out every FROM line across every build stage, and checks each release line against a small table checked into the tool -- no pull, no build, no browser tab per line. Every finding says whether the date is the project's own published end date (confirmed) or inferred from its stated support-length policy (estimated), and the table carries a snapshot date so you know how fresh it is.

Where each approach earns its keep.
SituationBetter fit
One Dockerfile, one FROM line, and you already know the project's policy.Checking by hand -- often faster than opening this page at all.
A multi-stage build, several services, or a monorepo with many Dockerfiles.This checker -- it reads every FROM line at once instead of one tab per line.
The base image is outside this tool's curated table, or tagged latest.Checking by hand -- the tool reports these as unknown rather than guessing.
A finding this tool marks estimated, and you want the project's own words.Both -- re-verify the specific finding against the upstream page rather than re-checking everything.

Treat this checker as the first pass across many FROM lines, and a manual read of the upstream page as the second pass on whichever findings matter enough to double-check. This page names no product or company being compared against -- checking a project's own release page by hand is a method, not a competitor.

Run the free base image EOL check

Common questions

Why not just look up each base image's end-of-life date myself?

You can, and for one Dockerfile with one FROM line it may be faster than pasting it in here. It stops scaling once there is more than one: a multi-stage build can name a different release on every FROM line, a monorepo can hold dozens of Dockerfiles, and each lookup means finding and reading the right project's own release notes or end-of-life policy correctly. This tool reads every FROM line in every file you paste at once and reports all of them against one dated table.

Is a manual lookup on the project's own release page more accurate than this tool's table?

It can be, since it is live and this tool's table is a checked-in snapshot with its own as-of date shown in the results. The tradeoff is throughput and consistency: a manual pass across many FROM lines takes one browser tab and one careful read per line, and it is easy to skip a stage in a multi-stage build or misread a policy page. This tool checks every line the same way, every time, and tells you plainly which findings are the project's own confirmed date versus an estimate inferred from its policy -- a distinction a quick manual read can blur.

Does this replace reading the base image's own release page?

No, and the page says so: re-verify any finding against the upstream project's own page before relying on it, especially an estimated one. What this tool replaces is doing that lookup for every FROM line in every Dockerfile, every time you want to know -- it narrows the manual work to the findings worth double-checking instead of every line you have.

What does a manual check catch that this tool cannot?

A base image or private-registry reference outside this tool's curated table, and a tag of latest, are both reported as unknown rather than guessed at -- a manual reader who knows the project can sometimes reason about those where the table stays silent. A manual reader can also catch a policy change the table's snapshot has not picked up yet, which is exactly why the results carry a snapshot date and a re-verify note.

what-to-do-when-a-base-image-is-eol.html.text:
← Docker Base Image EOL Check

What to do when a base image comes back end-of-life

An eol or deprecated-image finding is a prioritization signal, not an incident report. Here is how to triage findings across more than one Dockerfile, plan the upgrade rather than just bumping the tag, and what to document if you cannot upgrade today.

Triage by exposure first, by date second

A scan across a monorepo commonly returns several findings at once, and not every finding carries the same risk even at the same days-past-end-of-life count. Work the list in this order:

PriorityWhat it looks likeWhy it comes first
1 — highestAn internet-facing service, on a deprecated-image or eol findingDirectly reachable, and the release line is either discontinued outright or already unpatched
2An internal service handling untrusted input (uploads, webhooks, third-party feeds), on eolNot directly exposed, but processes data it does not control
3An internal batch job or CI-only image, on eolNarrower attack surface, but still unpatched and worth a planned upgrade
4 — lowestAny of the above on eol-soonStill supported today; the work is scheduling the upgrade before the date arrives, not an urgent fix

This tool does not know which of your services is internet-facing or what data it handles — it only classifies the base image reference. Apply your own exposure knowledge on top of its output; do not read the table above as a re-ranking the tool performs for you.

Plan the upgrade — a major-version bump is a real change

A patch-level bump within the same major release (node:18.19 to the latest node:18 point release) is usually safe to rebuild and ship. Moving across a major version line — node:18 to node:22, python:3.9 to python:3.12, an Ubuntu codename change — can change runtime defaults, drop deprecated APIs, or bring newer versions of whatever the base OS installs by default. Treat it the way you would any dependency major bump:

  1. Read the target release's own changelog or migration notes for breaking changes, not just its end-of-life date.
  2. Bump one Dockerfile or one stage at a time rather than a repo-wide find-and-replace, especially across a multi-stage build where a builder stage and a runtime stage can reasonably land on different release lines.
  3. Rebuild and run your existing test suite against the new image before merging — a clean build is not evidence the runtime behaves the same.
  4. Re-scan afterward. A successful upgrade should turn the finding into supported, not just move it further from today's date.

If you cannot upgrade today

Sometimes the upgrade is real work — a framework version tied to the runtime, a dependency that has not caught up yet, a freeze window. Three things are worth doing even when the fix has to wait:

  • Pin to the image's current exact content digest. This does not change its end-of-life status, but it stops the reference from silently moving further from the last point it was patched while you wait. See Docker Base Image Pin Check for that specific question.
  • Write the finding down somewhere durable. This tool's report lives in your browser tab and this page saves nothing on your behalf — open a ticket or note it in whatever tracks technical debt on your team, with the release line and the end-of-life date from the report.
  • Set a re-check date, and prefer wiring check.py --fail-on-risk into CI over relying on someone remembering to re-run this page. A documented, time-boxed exception is a defensible decision; an undocumented one is just drift.

Common questions

Does an end-of-life finding mean my image is already vulnerable?

No. It means the release line's publisher has stopped shipping security patches for it, so any vulnerability discovered from that date forward will not be fixed upstream. An image on that release line can still show a clean vulnerability scan today — the risk is that nobody is looking for new issues in it any more, not that a specific one is already known. Treat it as a prioritization signal, not an incident.

Which finding should I fix first?

Triage by exposure before you triage by how long a release has been end-of-life. An internet-facing service on an end-of-life image outranks an internal batch job on one that went end-of-life more recently, even if the batch job's finding looks more urgent by date alone. Within a tier, deprecated-image findings (a repository discontinued outright, not just a version that stopped getting patches) and eol findings outrank eol-soon warnings.

Can I just bump the tag and rebuild?

Sometimes, for a patch-level bump within the same major version. A bump across a major version line (node:18 to node:22, python:3.9 to python:3.12, an Ubuntu codename change) can carry breaking changes in the runtime or the base OS's own package versions, so treat it as a real change to test in CI, not a same-day find-and-replace across every Dockerfile that references the old tag.

What if I cannot upgrade right now?

Pin the current image to its exact content digest so it stops moving further from the point where it was last patched, note the finding somewhere it will not be forgotten (a ticket, not just this page's report, which nothing here saves for you), and set a re-check date. That is a documented, time-boxed exception, not a fix — the release line is still unpatched upstream for as long as the pin stands.

Want the accuracy question instead — where the dates come from and what a clean scan does and doesn't mean? See the tool's own FAQ, or how this compares to a vulnerability scanner and to checking end-of-life dates by hand.
